rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Torah’s account is accepted, the people also suffered lightning and thunder in addition to the stone hurling windstorm.
rows.anchor: If the statement of the Torah in this regard is also accepted, it will become further evident

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madyan lay on the Red Sea southeast of Sinai; Shuayb was sent to its people.
rows.anchor: The place inhabited by the nation of Madyan was along the shores of the Red Sea towards the south east of mount of Sina ī.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuayb was the man who married his daughter to Moses; Moses stayed with him for a long time and tended his flock, an account in al-Qasas.
rows.anchor: The Prophet Shu‘ayb (sws) was sent to them. He was the same person who had wedded his daughter with Moses (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madyan’s location on a major trade route made its people advanced in trade; after their beliefs corrupted, other vices common to trading societies arose.
rows.anchor: Since the people of Madyan lived along an important trade route, they had become very advanced in trade.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unspecified clear proof may have been a visible miracle, as God gave other messengers, but neither Qur’an nor Torah identifies it.
rows.anchor: The details of “the clear proof” referred to here are neither mentioned in the Qur’ ān nor in the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the clear proof may be Shuayb himself and his preaching: a messenger embodies conclusive evidence, leaving only the stubborn without grounds to deny it.
rows.anchor: It is also possible that this refers to his own self and his preaching.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miracles are secondary, not a requirement of prophethood; God may show one at a nation’s demand to make the truth conclusive.
rows.anchor: A miracle is not a requisite of prophethood; it is from among its secondary elements.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic preaching rests on clear proofs inherent in human nature and intellect; the prophet’s life, words, gestures, and actions embody them.
rows.anchor: The actual content of the preaching of a prophet is based on clear and conclusive proofs which are innately found in human nature and intellect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dishonest weights and measures are not an isolated offense but an expression of wider societal wrongdoing and the loss of justice and truth.
rows.anchor: Being dishonest in measuring and weighing is not an independent wrongdoing: it actually is an expression of many wrongdoings that are found in a nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The society-wide corruption appeared among Madyan’s traders as dishonest measurement and weighing, though it had infected the whole society.
rows.anchor: Since the people of Madyan were traders by profession, it manifested itself in them in the form of dishonesty in measurement and weighing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command against fraud is paired with a ban on spreading disorder because dishonest dealings disrupt society as a whole.
rows.anchor: they should not spread disorder in the land.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Social justice reflects the balance on which God established the heavens and earth; disturbing it threatens the order of society.
rows.anchor: God has set up the heavens and the earth on a scale.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Within people’s sphere of authority, a country’s system stands only while justice stands; injustice severs society’s connections.
rows.anchor: people will be able to establish the system of the country as long as they are able to establish justice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects the call for just measure with the balance and justice commanded in al-Rahman 55:7–9.
rows.anchor: In verses 7-9 of S ūrah al-Raḥmān, this fact is explained thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase after the land was set right recalls nations repeatedly disrupting truth and justice through rebellion, after which God restored the order.
rows.anchor: From the anecdote of Noah (sws) to that of Shu‘ayb (sws), the history of every nation bears witness to this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madyan received political authority after a corrupt system had been destroyed.
rows.anchor: The people of Madyan too were granted political authority after a corrupt system had been destroyed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madyan’s people descended from Abraham and claimed the guidance of earlier prophets, but altered it to fit their desires.
rows.anchor: they, in fact, belonged to the descendents of Abraham (sws) and claimed to be the carriers of the guidance of the previous prophets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuayb says that professed believers must prove their faith by stopping disorder and mending the affairs he calls them to mend.
rows.anchor: if they lay claim to faith, then to prove it they should desist from spreading disorder and take to mending affairs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning alludes to Madyan’s harmful schemes and intimidation intended to drive believers away from Shuayb and the way of faith.
rows.anchor: This is an allusion to the evil practices of his nation and how they would relish and plan in harming Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The path to God is monotheism; distorting it leads people to polytheism and error.
rows.anchor: The path to reach God is monotheism. If some tries to distort it, it will lead people to polytheism and they will go astray.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder that they were few and then increased calls for gratitude, while the reminder of wrongdoers’ fate warns the ungrateful.
rows.anchor: The first sentence invites people to express gratitude and the second depicts the fate of the ingrates.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From a small family in Abraham’s time, Madyan grew in population, means, and resources into a powerful, flourishing nation by the final Prophet’s advent.
rows.anchor: Not only did they increase in number, their means and resources also increased.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their God-given growth called for gratitude and obedience, but instead they were ungrateful, rebellious, and spread disorder after it had been set right.
rows.anchor: On the contrary, they have shown ingratitude and rebelliousness and are spreading disorder in the land of God after it had been set right.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nearby remnants of the destruction of Thamud and Lot’s nations were lessons for Madyan’s people.
rows.anchor: Close by them are the remnants of the signs of destruction of the nations of Tham ūd and Lot (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened fate is certain; God’s respite does not make Shuayb’s warning false, since every matter has its appointed time.
rows.anchor: The implication is that this fate is certain to befall them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives respite so that people beyond those already believing may still accept faith.
rows.anchor: The reason for this respite is that there may be others besides those who have already accepted faith who may also follow suit.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuayb invokes an established divine practice, which Islahi explains through the outcomes of messengers’ calls to their nations.
rows.anchor: In this verse, Shu‘ayb (sws) has referred to an established practice of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the majority rejects a messenger adamantly, it soon becomes clear the nation has no potential to accept faith, and punishment follows.
rows.anchor: becomes adamant on it. In this case, it soon becomes evident that this nation has no potential to accept faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When some accept and others oppose, the nation still has potential; God may extend its respite so more people can believe.
rows.anchor: It is possible that if more time is given to it, some more people may accept faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives a nation more time because He is merciful to creatures and slow to anger.
rows.anchor: Since God is extremely merciful to His creatures and takes time to show anger, He gives it some more time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nation’s respite also comes from the presence of its righteous people who accepted the messenger’s invitation.
rows.anchor: a nation gets this respite because of the presence of the righteous in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to wait includes patience: they should wait for a just decision announced at its proper time.
rows.anchor: The word “wait” here encompasses the meaning of patience.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant elements issue Shuayb and his companions a final warning; his answer passes over expulsion but squarely addresses the demand to return to their ways.
rows.anchor: This is the final warning to Shu‘ayb (sws) and his companions by the arrogant elements of their nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuayb’s answer decisively affirms faith and declares his aversion to the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: This is a very decisive answer. It has unrelenting resolve on faith and is also a proclamation of aversion to the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuayb regards the disbelievers’ ways as a pack of lies falsely attributed to God without proof.
rows.anchor: they consists of a pack of lies that have has been ascribed to God without any proof.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He asks why they would return to those ways after God’s grace delivered them from that curse.
rows.anchor: why should they return to their ways when God’s grace has delivered them from this curse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuayb answers on behalf of followers who had lived in error before believing, which explains the phrase about being delivered.
rows.anchor: Shu‘ayb (sws) is also answering on behalf of his followers who before accepting faith had lived a life of error.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers are guided by their nature even before their mission and are never tainted by polytheism.
rows.anchor: even before being called to their duty they are guided by their nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that return is impossible unless God wills combines firm resolve with trust in God, which Islahi calls the essence of monotheism.
rows.anchor: The first part expresses their determination and the second one their trust in God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s will prevails; success in trials depends on the impulse He grants, and only He knows each person’s ordained fate.
rows.anchor: Succeeding in His trials depends on the urge He provides. Only He knows what is ordained for who and what fate a person is going to meet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuayb and his followers trust God alone and pray that He judge fairly as the best of judges.
rows.anchor: it is their prayer to God that He judge them with fairness because He is the best of judges.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi links these words to Abraham’s matching statement in al-Anam 6:80.
rows.anchor: Precisely the same words were uttered by Abraham (sws) as cited in verse 80

rows.speaker: the arrogant elements
rows.claim: The arrogant leaders warn the poor believers that following Shuayb will bring them great loss.
rows.anchor: these arrogant elements were left with nothing to say to him; however, they vented their anger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elders leave great loss undefined, so its ambiguity can encompass anything; the phrase also sounds sympathetic, as if they explained the choice and believers failed to see their benefit.
rows.anchor: They did not explain what they meant by “great loss” because concealed in this ambiguity was everything.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording of the punishment occurs identically in the account of Salih’s people and states the punishment without specifying its nature.
rows.anchor: The second of the verses occurs in precisely the same words in the anecdote of the nation of Ṣāliḥ.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud 11:94 explains the punishment with al-sayhah, meaning a shout and thunder.
rows.anchor: which means a shout and thunder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuara 26:189 calls it the torment of the day of the canopy; viewed from afar, it looked like a column or mountain of dust or smoke.
rows.anchor: It is evident from this that looking from afar, the torment seemed like a column or mountain of dust or smoke.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi relates the torment of Lot’s people to a stone-hurling wind and says the ḥāṣib punishment combines rajfah, sayhah, and zullah.
rows.anchor: It is evident from the anecdote of Lot’s nation that it was visited by a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another Qur’anic passage indicates that Madyan suffered the same punishment as Lot’s people; Islahi begins citing Shuayb’s warning in Hud 11:89.
rows.anchor: From another instance of the Qur’ān also, it is evident that the same torment visited them as the one that visited Lots’ nation.
